cases.abstract: Vision Transformers combine attention with training and architectural choices, leaving open how much of their recognition performance a convolutional network can recover. We investigate this question by progressively redesigning ResNet into ConvNeXt without introducing attention. After strengthening the training recipe, the study changes stage computation and separates spatial mixing from channel mixing: depthwise convolutions act on narrow features before pointwise layers expand and recombine channels. This arrangement accommodates larger spatial kernels, while normalized stage transitions stabilize the final network. At 384 x 384 resolution, ConvNeXt-B trained on ImageNet-1K achieves 85.1% top-1 accuracy versus 84.5% for Swin-B and processes 95.7 versus 85.1 images per second on a V100 GPU. Scaling to ConvNeXt-XL with ImageNet-22K pretraining and ImageNet-1K fine-tuning yields 87.8% top-1 accuracy at the same resolution. Competitive results on COCO and ADE20K extend the comparison to detection and segmentation. Together, the redesign and evaluations show that competitive recognition backbones can incorporate Transformer-style organization without relying on self-attention.
cases.methods: Large spatial kernels become expensive when applied after a block expands its channels. ConvNeXt instead places a 7 x 7 depthwise convolution first, mixing spatial information separately within each channel at the narrower input width. Layer normalization then precedes two 1 x 1 convolutions that expand width fourfold and restore it, with one GELU between them and a residual connection around the block. The ordering reserves expanded features for dense channel mixing while keeping the spatial operation inexpensive. A nonoverlapping 4 x 4 stem and separate, normalized downsampling connect the stages. The redesign is evaluated sequentially on ImageNet-1K using a fixed 300-epoch AdamW recipe, roughly controlled FLOPs, and three-seed averages in the ResNet-50 regime. This keeps the training recipe constant across architectural steps, while allowing the measured effect of a change to depend on the configuration already reached.
cases.results: The modernization results favor coordinated redesign over assuming that every Transformer-inspired substitution improves a ConvNet. Modern training raises ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy from 76.1% to 78.8% before the architecture changes. With that recipe fixed, replacing ReLU with GELU leaves accuracy at 80.6%, whereas reducing the block to one activation raises it to 81.3%. The contrast favors simplifying activation placement in this configuration, not merely adopting a Transformer-associated activation. Separating downsampling from residual blocks causes divergence until normalization is added around resolution changes and after pooling; the resulting roadmap model reaches 82.0%, versus Swin-T's 81.3%. Each comparison is conditional on preceding modifications. Transfer evaluation tests whether the redesigned backbone's competitiveness extends beyond classification: with ImageNet-22K pretraining and Cascade Mask R-CNN under a 3x schedule, ConvNeXt-B reaches 54.0 box AP and 46.9 mask AP on COCO, versus Swin-B's 53.0 and 45.8. The classification sequence and transfer comparison support the combined design while distinguishing useful changes from neutral or unstable intermediate configurations.
cases.notes: Final Text Check: abstract connects attention-free redesign to recognition comparisons (Table 1); Methods ties narrow-channel spatial convolution to affordable larger kernels (Sections 2.3-2.5); Results tests design dependence and transfer (Sections 2.1, 2.6; Table 3). Roadmap accuracy is 82.0%, not the main table's 82.1%; these remain separate records. Successive changes do not isolate independent component effects. ImageNet-1K training is distinct from ImageNet-22K pretraining and fine-tuning. EfficientNetV2-L has the highest listed ImageNet-1K-only accuracy, so the advantage remains scoped to Swin. No significance claim follows from seed means.

cases.abstract: Fast radiance-field training does not by itself deliver interactive rendering at high reconstruction quality. We represent a static scene with anisotropic 3D Gaussians initialized from sparse structure-from-motion points, each carrying opacity and spherical-harmonic appearance. Projecting these primitives to image-space splats supports differentiable rendering without estimating surface normals. Adaptive cloning and splitting refine inadequate geometry, while a tile-based rasterizer replaces per-pixel sorting with shared depth-ordered lists and propagates gradients without a fixed primitive-count cutoff. On held-out photographs from Mip-NeRF360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending, the 30,000-iteration configuration renders at dataset-average rates of 134-154 frames per second on an A6000 GPU after approximately 27-42 minutes of training. It exceeds Mip-NeRF360 in SSIM across these datasets, but has lower PSNR on the Mip-NeRF360 dataset. The method therefore combines real-time rendering with competitive, metric-dependent reconstruction quality rather than uniform superiority. Stored parameters occupy hundreds of megabytes, substantially more than the neural baselines; weakly observed regions remain artifact-prone, and approximate visibility can produce popping as the viewpoint changes.
cases.methods: Sorting overlapping splats separately at every pixel and storing each pixel's blending history would make differentiable rendering costly. The renderer projects Gaussian covariances into image space, assigns splat instances to 16 x 16 pixel tiles, and uses keys combining tile identity and view-space depth for one GPU radix sort. Each tile reuses the resulting ordered list while its pixels blend front to back until opacity saturation. This avoids per-pixel sorting, although the shared order approximates visibility. During backpropagation, reverse traversal of the same lists reconstructs intermediate opacity factors from saved final accumulations, avoiding variable-length per-pixel histories without imposing a fixed primitive-count limit on gradients. A combined L1 and D-SSIM image loss updates geometry, opacity, and appearance. Between updates, positional gradients select small Gaussians for cloning or large ones for splitting, allowing sparse initial coverage to acquire additional geometric detail.
cases.results: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, increasing optimization from 7,000 to 30,000 iterations raises PSNR from 25.60 to 27.21 dB and lowers LPIPS from 0.279 to 0.214, but rendering drops from 160 to 134 frames per second and stored parameters grow from 523 to 734 MB. Better reconstruction therefore comes with a larger model and lower throughput. Relative to the published Mip-NeRF360 reference, the longer-trained model has higher SSIM and lower LPIPS but lower PSNR, so the quality advantage depends on the metric. Its approximately 42-minute training on an A6000 should not be interpreted as a matched-GPU speedup over Mip-NeRF360's reported 48 GPU-hours, obtained from four A100s running for 12 hours. A separate three-scene ablation tests whether gradient propagation can be cheaply truncated: limiting updates to ten frontmost Gaussians lowers average 30,000-iteration PSNR from 26.05 to 19.19 dB across Truck, Garden, and Bicycle. This shortcut substantially compromises reconstruction in that evaluation. Poor coverage artifacts and occasional popping also remain despite the full renderer's speed.
cases.notes: Final Text Check: abstract connects projected primitives and shared sorting to fast rendering (Sections 4-6; Table 1); Methods explains sorting and backward-history costs (Section 6); Results tests the quality-resource tradeoff and gradient cutoff (Tables 1, 3). Every eighth photograph is held out. Mip-NeRF360 metrics on its dataset are adopted; other dataset metrics are reruns. Its 48 GPU-hours are a single-GPU-equivalent total from four A100s, not A6000 wall time. Ablations use separately downsampled high-resolution inputs. Table 1 memory counts stored parameters, excluding training peaks and rasterizer workspace. Synthetic random-initialization success does not extend to poorly constrained real captures.
